SEC Charges Former Hedge Fund Analyst With Insider Trading Ahead of Merger

Published 2026-10-06 19:00 UTC

Washington D.C., Oct. 6, 2026 The Securities and Exchange Commission today charged Daniel Okafor, a former analyst at a New York hedge fund, with insider trading ahead of the announced acquisition of Corvel Therapeutics by a large pharmaceutical company.

According to the SEC's complaint, Okafor learned of the confidential merger negotiations through his work and bought out-of-the-money call options in Corvel days before the deal was announced, generating illegal profits of approximately $480,000. He also allegedly tipped a friend, who made an additional $210,000.

The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Manhattan, charges Okafor with violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws and seeks disgorgement, civil penalties and an officer-and-director bar. In a parallel action, the U.S. Attorney's Office announced criminal charges.

According to the SEC's complaint, the analyst learned confidential information about the pending acquisition through his work at a hedge fund that was advising on financing for the deal. Within days, he allegedly bought out-of-the-money call options in the target company through an account in a relative's name.

When the merger was publicly announced, the target company's stock price rose more than 35%, and the analyst allegedly made profits of approximately $1.8 million. The SEC's market surveillance group detected the unusual options activity shortly before the announcement and referred the matter for investigation.

The complaint charges the analyst with violating the antifraud provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The SEC seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of profits with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty. In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office announced criminal charges against the analyst.

The SEC thanked the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority for its assistance. The investigation was conducted by the Division of Enforcement's Market Abuse Unit, which uses data analytics to identify suspicious trading ahead of corporate announcements.
